accepted_examples.german: Es ist furchtbar kalt heute.
accepted_examples.english: It's awfully cold today.
accepted_examples.note: furchtbar is used as an intensifier meaning awfully/terribly, and both languages express the same degree of cold.

accepted_examples.german: Draußen ist’s heiß. Lass uns also drinnen sprechen!
accepted_examples.english: It's hot outside, so let's talk inside.
accepted_examples.note: drinnen means inside; the contrast with draußen and the English translation align.

accepted_examples.german: Lass etwas Kuchen für uns andere übrig.
accepted_examples.english: Leave some cake for the rest of us.
accepted_examples.note: übrig means remaining/left over, matching the request to leave cake for the rest of the group.

accepted_examples.german: Die Polizei schaute überall und konnte keine Spur von Tom finden.
accepted_examples.english: The police looked everywhere and couldn't find any trace of Tom.
accepted_examples.note: Spur means trace in the sense of a sign of someone’s presence; the English translation matches.

accepted_examples.german: Die Flasche bitte nicht aus dem Fenster werfen!
accepted_examples.english: Please don't throw the bottle out the window.
accepted_examples.note: werfen is used as the infinitive after bitte nicht and means throw, exactly as translated.

accepted_examples.german: Er heißt Tom, und er ist Marias Ehemann.
accepted_examples.english: His name is Tom and he's Mary's husband.
accepted_examples.note: Ehemann means husband; the possessive Marias and English possessive agree.

accepted_examples.german: Die drohen damit, die Geiseln zu erschießen.
accepted_examples.english: They're threatening to shoot the hostages.
accepted_examples.note: erschießen means shoot dead; the sentence and translation describe a threat to kill by shooting.

accepted_examples.german: Geben Sie Ihren Namen und Ihre Adresse an.
accepted_examples.english: Fill in your name and address.
accepted_examples.note: Adresse means address; the formal instruction and translation convey the same action.

accepted_examples.german: Das ist Unsinn. Nur ein Narr würde es glauben.
accepted_examples.english: That's nonsense. Nobody but a fool would believe it.
accepted_examples.note: Unsinn means nonsense, with the same claim in both languages.

accepted_examples.german: Du bist die einzige, die mir Respekt entgegenbringt.
accepted_examples.english: You're the only person who shows me any respect.
accepted_examples.note: Respekt is the noun respect, and entgegenbringen is correctly translated as show.

accepted_examples.german: Es kam zu einer Schwierigkeit nach der anderen.
accepted_examples.english: One difficulty after another arose.
accepted_examples.note: Schwierigkeit means difficulty/problem; the sentence and translation convey repeated problems arising.

accepted_examples.german: Der Jupiter ist der größte Planet des Sonnensystems.
accepted_examples.english: Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System.
accepted_examples.note: Planet is used for Jupiter in the astronomical sense, with a matching superlative.

accepted_examples.german: Der Lehrer stand in der Mitte der Gruppe.
accepted_examples.english: The teacher stood in the middle of the group.
accepted_examples.note: Gruppe means group, and the sentence and translation agree.

accepted_examples.german: Tom hat wirklich einen schlechten Deal bekommen.
accepted_examples.english: Tom really got a bad deal.
accepted_examples.note: Deal means a deal/transaction; schlecht selects the same negative sense in English.

accepted_examples.german: Hast du irgendwelche Sachen, die du nie anziehst?
accepted_examples.english: Do you have any clothes that you never wear?
accepted_examples.note: irgendwelche means any/no matter which in this question about clothes.

accepted_examples.german: Ich hätte es gerne mit jeder Menge Eis.
accepted_examples.english: I want it with plenty of ice.
accepted_examples.note: Eis is used as ice in a food/drink context, matching the translation.

accepted_examples.german: Hast du schon etwas für das Wochenende vor?
accepted_examples.english: Do you have any plans for the weekend?
accepted_examples.note: Wochenende means weekend; the question asks about plans for that weekend.

accepted_examples.german: Das ist es, worüber wir uns Sorgen machen.
accepted_examples.english: That's what we're worried about.
accepted_examples.note: worüber introduces the topic of the concern; the English worried about preserves the prepositional sense.

accepted_examples.german: Tom hat Mühe, auf einem Bein zu stehen.
accepted_examples.english: Tom has trouble standing on one leg.
accepted_examples.note: Bein means leg in the body-part sense, and the balance sentence translates directly.

accepted_examples.german: Das ist ein Verbrechen.
accepted_examples.english: That's a felony.
accepted_examples.note: Verbrechen means a serious crime; felony is a context-appropriate English rendering.

accepted_examples.german: Wie oft hörst du nachts die Wölfe heulen?
accepted_examples.english: How often do you hear wolves howling at night?
accepted_examples.note: nachts means at night, matching the time in the sentence.

accepted_examples.german: Das waren die schlimmsten Schmerzen, die ich je erlebt habe.
accepted_examples.english: That was the worst pain I have ever felt.
accepted_examples.note: Schmerz appears in its plural Schmerzen for physical pain; the bilingual pair refers to the same experience.

accepted_examples.german: Sie ging gleich ans Telefon, als sie es klingeln hörte.
accepted_examples.english: She answered the telephone as soon as she heard the bell ring.
accepted_examples.note: klingeln means ring/make a bell sound, and the sentence and translation describe hearing the telephone ring.

accepted_examples.german: Der Wettkampf um diese Position ist sehr intensiv.
accepted_examples.english: Competition for the position is very intense.
accepted_examples.note: Position means position/post, matching the competition for a role.

accepted_examples.german: Ihr scheint die gleichen Probleme wie ich zu haben.
accepted_examples.english: It looks like you have the same problems I do.
accepted_examples.note: gleichen means resemble/be like; the comparison of problems is the same in both languages.

accepted_examples.german: Hast du dir im Fernsehen das Fußballspiel angesehen?
accepted_examples.english: Did you watch the match on television?
accepted_examples.note: Fernsehen means television; the sentence refers to watching a football match on television.

accepted_examples.german: Also habt ihr schließlich doch beschlossen zu kommen.
accepted_examples.english: So, you decided to come after all.
accepted_examples.note: schließlich means finally/after all; the sentence’s doch and the English after all express the same conclusion.

accepted_examples.german: Das ist der Fisch, den er gefangen hat.
accepted_examples.english: This is the fish he caught.
accepted_examples.note: gefangen is the participle of fangen and means caught, matching the relative clause.

accepted_examples.german: Dieses Buch ist zu schwierig für mich.
accepted_examples.english: This book is too difficult for me to understand.
accepted_examples.note: schwierig means difficult; the book is described as too difficult for the speaker.

accepted_examples.german: Wir waren gezwungen, Toms Angebot anzunehmen.
accepted_examples.english: We were forced to accept Tom's proposal.
accepted_examples.note: Angebot means proposal/offer; Tom’s proposal is what they were forced to accept.

accepted_examples.german: Er steckte Maria den Ring an den Finger.
accepted_examples.english: He put the ring on Mary's finger.
accepted_examples.note: Ring means a circular piece of jewelry here, matching the English translation.

accepted_examples.german: Haben Sie schon einmal dieses Lied gehört, auf Französisch gesungen?
accepted_examples.english: Have you ever heard that song sung in French?
accepted_examples.note: Lied means a sung musical composition; the French-language performance is described in both versions.

accepted_examples.german: Sorry, dass ich deine Party verpasst habe.
accepted_examples.english: I'm sorry I missed your party.
accepted_examples.note: sorry is used as an apology for missing the party, the same function as in English.

accepted_examples.german: Es sieht fantastisch aus.
accepted_examples.english: It looks fantastic.
accepted_examples.note: fantastisch means fantastic, and the sentence and translation are direct equivalents.

accepted_examples.german: Der Fuchs tappt nicht zweimal in dieselbe Falle.
accepted_examples.english: A fox isn't caught twice in the same snare.
accepted_examples.note: Falle means trap/snare in the proverb; the English translation is equivalent.

accepted_examples.german: Es sieht so aus, als hättest du einen Drink nötig.
accepted_examples.english: You look like you could use a drink.
accepted_examples.note: Drink means an alcoholic drink in this idiomatic English rendering; nötig makes the context fit.

accepted_examples.german: Auf der Insel gibt es nur eine Straße.
accepted_examples.english: There's only one road on the island.
accepted_examples.note: Insel means island and is used in the same geographic sense in both languages.

accepted_examples.german: Wir sind uns rein zufällig begegnet.
accepted_examples.english: Our meeting was purely accidental.
accepted_examples.note: zufällig means by chance/accidentally; the meeting is described as accidental in English.

accepted_examples.german: Was ist der Unterschied zwischen einem Dorf und einer Stadt?
accepted_examples.english: What's the difference between a village and a town?
accepted_examples.note: Dorf means village; the comparison with a town is translated accurately.

held_examples.german: Nie, solange ich lebe, werde ich dir verzeihen!
held_examples.reason: The German sentence says the speaker will forgive the person, while the English says the opposite; the pair reverses the meaning.

held_examples.german: Ich habe Tom als „fettes Schwein“ tituliert.
held_examples.reason: The candidate is an insulting expression directed at a person, not a neutral animal example for the entry.

held_examples.german: Ganz unter uns: sie ist wirklich ein Monster.
held_examples.reason: The candidate uses monster as a personal insult; a neutral fictional-creature context is clearer for learners.

held_examples.german: Laß uns so weit vorne wie möglich sitzen!
held_examples.reason: The sentence uses superseded spelling Laß; use current standard spelling in learner-facing material.

held_examples.german: Tom hat ein Messer in der Hand.
held_examples.reason: Messer means knife in this sentence, but the selected entry sense is measurer/surveyor.

held_examples.german: Eine neue Studie besagt, daß Kaffee gesund ist.
held_examples.reason: The German uses superseded spelling daß; use current standard spelling.

held_examples.german: Leiste nur weiterhin so gute Arbeit.
held_examples.reason: Leiste is a verb form of leisten here, not the noun Leiste in the selected entry.

held_examples.german: Ich habe eine Thermoskanne Kaffee gemacht, so dass ihr ihn mitnehmen könnt zu eurem Imbiss.
held_examples.reason: The German phrasing zu eurem Imbiss is awkward and the English lunch does not accurately match Imbiss.

held_examples.german: Ich bin nicht hier, um Freundschaften zu schließen.
held_examples.reason: schließen means make something no longer open here; the source instead uses the different idiom Freundschaften schließen.

held_examples.german: Die Prinzessin konnte nicht umhin, seiner zu lachen.
held_examples.reason: The German construction seiner zu lachen is ungrammatical for the meaning in the English translation.
Bulle can also mean a police officer; the sentence gives no livestock context to disambiguate the intended animal sense.

editorial_examples.german: Ich hoffe, dass du mir eines Tages verzeihen kannst.
editorial_examples.english: I hope that you can forgive me one day.
editorial_examples.note: A neutral, direct example of verzeihen with a clear dative object.

editorial_examples.german: Das Schwein liegt im Stroh und ruht sich aus.
editorial_examples.english: The pig is lying in the straw and resting.
editorial_examples.note: A neutral farm-animal context avoids using Schwein as an insult.

editorial_examples.german: Im Märchen lebt ein freundliches Monster unter der Brücke.
editorial_examples.english: A friendly monster lives under the bridge in the fairy tale.
editorial_examples.note: A neutral fictional-creature context demonstrates the noun without insulting a person.

editorial_examples.german: Lass uns so weit vorne wie möglich sitzen.
editorial_examples.english: Let’s sit as close to the front as we can.
editorial_examples.note: The revised sentence uses current standard spelling.

editorial_examples.german: Der Messer nahm die Maße des Grundstücks auf.
editorial_examples.english: The surveyor measured the plot of land.
editorial_examples.note: This uses Messer in the selected, less common sense of a person who measures.
A short contemporary sentence with current spelling and a direct translation.

editorial_examples.german: Die Leiste an der Wand verdeckt die Kante des Bodens.
editorial_examples.english: The trim along the wall covers the edge of the floor.
editorial_examples.note: This demonstrates the noun Leiste as a strip of trim.

editorial_examples.english: Please take an umbrella with you.
editorial_examples.note: A concise, natural example of separable mitnehmen.

editorial_examples.german: Bitte schließen Sie die Tür hinter sich.
editorial_examples.english: Please close the door behind you.
editorial_examples.note: This demonstrates the selected meaning of schließen directly.

editorial_examples.german: Die Prinzessin konnte nicht aufhören, über den Witz zu lachen.
editorial_examples.english: The princess could not stop laughing at the joke.
editorial_examples.note: The replacement is grammatical and aligns directly with the English translation.

editorial_examples.german: Der Bulle grast mit der Herde auf der Weide.
editorial_examples.english: The bull is grazing with the herd in the pasture.
editorial_examples.note: The pasture context makes the livestock sense unambiguous.
